slide.heading: Pharmacodynamics
slide.subheading: What a drug does to the body

lines.text: Good morning, everyone. Let's get started.
Today is pharmacodynamics: what a drug does to the body. Pharmacokinetics, what the body does to the drug, is a separate lecture.
By the end, you should be able to read a dose-response curve and explain what it tells you about a drug, and about your patient.

slide.heading: Receptors and ligands
bullets: Most drugs act by binding a target protein, often a receptor
A ligand is anything that binds it: drug, hormone or neurotransmitter
Most drug binding is reversible
Affinity: how tightly it binds (Kd = 50% occupancy)

lines.text: Most drugs work by binding a specific target protein. Very often, that target is a receptor.
Anything that binds the receptor is called a ligand: the drug, but also the body's own hormones and neurotransmitters.
Most of this binding is reversible. Molecules attach and detach constantly, so how many receptors are occupied depends on concentration.
How tightly a ligand binds is its affinity. We describe it with Kd, the concentration at which half the receptors are occupied. A lower Kd means higher affinity.

slide.heading: Agonists
bullets: Bind the receptor and activate it
Full agonist: can produce the maximal response
Partial agonist: lower maximum, even at full occupancy
Intrinsic activity: how well binding becomes response

lines.text: An agonist binds the receptor and activates it. Binding alone isn't the point; activation is what produces the response.
A full agonist can drive the system all the way to its maximal response.
A partial agonist binds the same receptor but produces a smaller maximal response, even when every receptor is occupied.
I've drawn these two at the same potency so you can compare the plateaus. The partial agonist's lower ceiling reflects its intrinsic activity. More drug won't raise it.

slide.heading: Antagonists
bullets: Bind the receptor without activating it
No effect of their own when no agonist is present
They act by blocking an agonist
Two patterns: competitive and noncompetitive

lines.text: An antagonist binds the receptor but doesn't activate it.
With no agonist around, a pure antagonist does nothing visible. Its effect comes from stopping an agonist, whether a drug or the body's own ligand, from acting.
How it blocks matters. The two patterns you need to know are competitive and noncompetitive antagonism.

slide.heading: Competitive antagonism
bullets: Reversible binding at the agonist's site
Surmountable: more agonist restores the full response
Curve shifts right, in parallel
EC50 increases; Emax is unchanged

lines.text: A competitive antagonist binds reversibly to the same site the agonist uses. The two compete for every receptor.
Add enough agonist and it outcompetes the antagonist. We call that surmountable.
On the graph, that's a parallel shift to the right. You need more agonist for the same effect, so the EC50 goes up, but the maximal response is unchanged.

steps.intro: Let's see it happen. Use the agonist control to raise the concentration until the response is close to its maximum.
steps.antagonist: Good. Now I'm adding a competitive antagonist at a fixed concentration. Watch the receptors, and watch your response drop.
steps.predict: Before you touch anything, make a prediction.
steps.test: Now test it. Keep raising the agonist concentration and watch the response.
steps.wrap: Same maximum, but it took about ten times more agonist: the EC50 moved from 1 to 10. That parallel, rightward shift is competitive antagonism.

lines.text: Remember that picture. When more agonist wins back the full effect, think competitive.

slide.heading: Noncompetitive antagonism
bullets: Irreversible binding, or binding at an allosteric site
Not surmountable by adding more agonist
Emax decreases
Classic picture: EC50 of remaining receptors about the same

lines.text: A noncompetitive antagonist either binds irreversibly, often covalently, or binds a separate allosteric site that stops the receptor responding.
Either way, adding more agonist can't fix it. Those receptors are out of play.
So the maximal response drops. In the classic textbook picture, the plateau falls while the EC50 stays about the same.

slide.heading: Potency
bullets: How much drug is needed for a given effect
Compared using EC50
Lower EC50 = more potent = curve further left
Changes the dose, not what the drug can achieve

lines.text: Potency tells you how much drug you need to get a given effect.
We compare potency using the EC50: the concentration that produces half of that drug's own maximal effect.
Drug A reaches half its maximum at a lower concentration than Drug B, so A is more potent. On the graph, more potent means further to the left.
But potency mostly changes the dose you prescribe, not how much the drug can ultimately do.

slide.heading: Efficacy
bullets: The maximal effect a drug can produce (Emax)
Read from the height of the plateau
A more potent drug can be less efficacious
When a large effect is needed, efficacy usually matters more

lines.text: Efficacy is the maximal effect a drug can produce: the height of the plateau.
Here, Drug B is more potent because its curve rises earlier, but Drug A reaches a higher maximum. A is more efficacious.
Keep the two separate. Potency is where the curve sits; efficacy is how high it goes.
When you need a large effect, efficacy is usually the property that matters most.

slide.heading: Dose-response relationships
bullets: Graded: one patient or tissue, response rises with dose
Plotted against log dose, the curve is sigmoid
Quantal: fraction of a population responding (ED50, TD50)
Therapeutic index = TD50 / ED50

lines.text: A graded dose-response curve follows one patient or one tissue: as the dose rises, the response grows.
Plot it against the log of the dose and you get the familiar S-shape, which makes EC50 and Emax easy to read.
A quantal curve asks something different: what fraction of a population shows a defined response at each dose? The dose that works in half of them is the ED50.
Do the same for a toxic effect and you get the TD50. The therapeutic index is TD50 divided by ED50. The larger it is, the wider the margin of safety.

slide.heading: Clinical application
bullets: Naloxone: competitive opioid antagonist, reverses overdose
It can wear off before the opioid does, so monitor
Buprenorphine: high-affinity partial μ-opioid agonist
Narrow therapeutic index, e.g. warfarin: monitor closely

lines.text: Let's make this clinical. A patient arrives after an opioid overdose. Naloxone, a competitive antagonist at opioid receptors, displaces the opioid and can reverse the respiratory depression.
Naloxone often wears off before the opioid does, so these patients need observation. Breathing can slow again.

Buprenorphine is a partial agonist that binds mu-opioid receptors with high affinity. In someone dependent on a full agonist, it can displace that drug while activating the receptor less, and precipitate withdrawal.
And for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, like warfarin, small changes in dose or blood level matter a lot, so we monitor closely.

slide.heading: Summary
bullets: Agonists activate; antagonists block
Competitive: right shift, same Emax
Noncompetitive: lower Emax
Potency = where the curve sits; efficacy = how high it goes

lines.text: So: agonists activate and antagonists block. Competitive antagonists shift the curve right; noncompetitive ones lower the ceiling.
Potency is where the curve sits, efficacy is how high it goes, and the therapeutic index tells you the margin of safety.
That's the framework. Hold on to it; you'll use it constantly.
